comparator.name: Economie en Bedrijfseconomie
comparator.sourceNotes: Verified on 27 October 2026 against the current programme page and adopted TiSEM EER v4, pp61–64, for the 2026 entrant cohort. The Dutch full-time bachelor has 180 EC. Both formal branches are equally broad; the neutral official-order tie-break selects Bedrijfseconomie. Required common and branch-specific courses are retained. Financiële Administratie (324928-B-6) is the selected 6-EC restricted elective. The 30-EC approved mobility/minor window remains unspecified. GROW is zero-credit extracurricular development; later semesters explicitly describe it as noncompulsory and strongly recommended. EER3.7 governs choice-space approval and nonoverlap. Article4.5 requires120EC for the sixth-semester thesis,138EC from semester7 and90EC for internship,with applicable manual/syllabus requirements. The positive BSA threshold is42first-yearEC;Article4.4 governs postponed-BSA progression. Article4.7 permits attendance conditions for assessed practical exercises,announced in OSIRIS/Canvas.
components: Choice among exchange, a 24 -ECTS internship plus a 6 -ECTS elective, Economics and Management minors, or another Tilburg minor.
Compulsory third-year course for the selected Bedrijfseconomie specialisation.
Selected 6-EC restricted elective (324928-B-6) from the adopted six-course list; coherent with the Bedrijfseconomie accounting/finance route.

courses: Business & Economy in the Age of AI
New Issues in Contemporary Social Theory

core: Microeconomics, consumer choice, strategic behaviour and market interaction
Macroeconomics, inflation, international trade, crises and inequality
Business economics, accounting, investment, corporate finance and financial risk
Mathematics, data analysis, AI, business intelligence and research methods
Public policy, taxation, labour, housing and economic institutions
Marketing, organisation, strategy and business administration
Sustainability, energy transition, business ethics and responsible governance
adjacent: Public economics, institutions, labour, inequality and environmental policy
Financial markets, corporate finance, banking, risk and sustainable finance
questions: How do consumers, firms and governments interact, and why do economic outcomes differ?
How can policy address inflation, housing, labour markets, trade and the energy transition?
How should firms balance investment, financial risk, sustainability and profitability?

trace: Financial statements and accounting information analyse how economic events affect businesses; not a separate advanced corporate-finance sequence.
AI impacts on competitiveness, labour, growth, inequality and governance directly examine technological economic change.
Financial-data cases, investment, budgeting and risk assessment implement practical financial decisions; the profile does not establish specialist monetary theory or asset pricing.
Microeconomic consumer/firm/market analysis and macroeconomic output, inflation and unemployment establish economic foundations.
Fiscal and monetary policy, cycles, crises and trade directly implement macroeconomic-policy inquiry.
Uncertainty, consumer behaviour, strategic interaction, factor markets, externalities and government implement microeconomic choice and policy analysis.
Market failure, public goods, taxation, spending and redistribution directly analyse efficiency, equity and public resource choices.
OLS, GLS, instrumental variables, tests, Stata simulations and an empirical paper implement causal/predictive economic research.
Biases, heuristics, framing and experiments provide substantive behavioural economic analysis.
Customer-needs investigation, product concept, costs/proceeds and environmental-impact assessment link firm choices to markets and sustainability.
Consumer psychology, marketing plans, brands, digital marketing and responsible customer engagement implement the marketing direction.
Strategic plans, business models and responsible digital transformation examine firm strategy under technological change.
Gathering customer evidence, analysing results and managerial recommendations apply research to market decisions.
Cross-border institutions, trade, geopolitics and corporate responsibility examine the environment of global firms; not company-law training.
Venture design, market validation, business planning and stakeholder-facing teamwork develop applied business foundations; not an organisation-theory substitute.
Design, operationalisation, sampling, inference and an applied group project provide empirical-methods foundations.
Motivation, groups, leadership, culture, power and organisational change give a concrete organisation/management contribution.
Planning under uncertainty, partial observability and resource constraints provides computational decision tools; not specialist financial-risk mathematics.
Relational theory, SQL, normalisation and query processing organise economic/business data; this complements business intelligence rather than reproducing it.
Data cleaning, manipulation, visualisation and an empirical project implement economic/business-data analysis.
Regression, classification, resampling, regularisation, trees and clustering provide predictive-analysis methods; not an identical Tilburg data-analysis syllabus.
Python programming, discrete concepts, testing and projects provide computational analysis skills; not R-language equivalence.
Differentiation, integration and differential equations provide mathematical tools for economic models and later statistics.
Matrices, linear systems, transformations, eigenvectors and Markov chains support multivariate models and quantitative economic analysis.
Multidimensional calculus, differential equations and computer algebra extend quantitative modelling tools.
Probability, distributions, estimation and simulation give mathematical foundations for statistical economic inference.
Policy enforcement, actors, interests and governance cases on energy, food, water and climate directly implement the evidenced energy/sustainability-policy direction.
Legal systems, public law, law/society and justice provide the gateway for analysing formal public institutions.
Comparative constitutional/administrative law analyses government powers, rights and institutional constraints on economic policy.
Ethical theories applied to inequality, wealth, future generations and climate develop normative evaluation of economic choices.
Authority, political power and normative political arguments support evaluation of economic-policy institutions.
States, political institutions, democracy and government capacity establish institutional conditions of public economic choices.
EU policy-making, interest groups, business influence and legislative research examine concrete economic governance.
Class, gender, race, institutions and major sociological theories support social analysis of distribution and economic problems.
Qualitative design, collection, interpretation and dissemination support empirical inquiry into policy actors and economic experience.
Modernity, imperialism and colonial responses provide the social-theory progression used to analyse institutions and civil society.
Civil society, social capital, trust, solidarity and NGO field inquiry analyse nonstate institutions shaping policy and distribution.
Regression, factor analysis, AN(C)OVA, logistic models and reporting support multivariate behavioural/market research; not a clinical-psychology claim.

EU legal institutions, fundamental rights, citizenship and free movement of workers, goods and establishments provide a specific legal-institutional contribution to economic integration and market governance.

alternatives.label: Economics, business & data
alternatives.labelReason: The completed UCR curriculum is broader than pure economics: it combines micro- and macroeconomics with accounting, finance, marketing, strategy, organisational study, data science, econometrics and international business.
alternatives.concept: A broad closest feasible response combining micro- and macroeconomics with accounting, finance, strategy, organisations, marketing, statistics, data, AI and research methods.
progression: Business, economics, data, research, mathematical and strategic foundations precede the advanced policy, organisational, international-business, machine-learning, econometrics, behavioural-economics, market-research and finance work. Strategy follows Business Foundations; Probability & Statistics follows Mathematical Methods; Money, Banking & Finance follows business, accounting and economic study. All formal prerequisites occur earlier and all courses are offered in their assigned terms.
traceOverrides: provides multivariate statistics and experimental methods that strengthen empirical economic and business research

alternatives.label: Economics, public institutions & social policy
alternatives.labelReason: Six economics courses and quantitative/qualitative methods form the core; political/legal institutions, civil society and sustainability governance apply that analysis to social policy. This does not claim specialised labour or housing economics.
alternatives.concept: Economic theory and empirical methods examine public spending, distribution, incentives and economic change. Political and legal institutions, civil society and sustainability governance provide concrete ways to investigate how economic choices become public decisions.
alternatives.distinctness: Compared with the business-and-data option, this programme gives substantial weight to comparative politics, public and EU law, social theory, qualitative inquiry and sustainability governance. EU law supplies concrete analysis of market integration and the movement of workers, goods and establishments; these courses implement the evidenced economic-institutions direction.
progression: Research Methods precedes all formal economics prerequisites; Mathematical Methods precedes Probability & Statistics; Law, Society & Justice precedes Comparative Constitutional Law. Introduction to Sociology and Modern Sociology precede contemporary civil-society theory.

alternatives.label: Finance, risk & quantitative analysis
alternatives.labelReason: The completed curriculum is organised around finance and economics with substantial mathematics, programming, data, econometrics and optimisation, rather than implying a specialist finance degree without a quantitative core.
alternatives.concept: Economics and practical financial decision-making are combined with econometrics, probability, calculus, programming, databases, machine learning and computational planning under uncertainty. Quantitative methods support economic and financial inquiry; they are not specialised asset-pricing or financial-risk courses.
alternatives.distinctness: Compared with the first programme, programming, relational databases, computational planning, linear algebra and advanced calculus replace experimental methods, marketing, consumer-product development, organisational psychology and market research. This is a real shift toward quantitative economic/financial inquiry; compared with the policy option, it retains business and financial foundations instead of the political/legal/social-policy strand.
progression: Business Foundations precedes Strategy & Digital Transformation and Money, Banking & Finance. Mathematical Methods precedes Probability & Statistics, Linear Algebra and Advanced Calculus; programming precedes computational decision-making; accounting, economics, data and research foundations precede the final finance, econometrics and behavioural-economics work. All formal prerequisites occur earlier and all courses are offered in their assigned terms.

routeSelection.basis: The generic exact target contains two equally broad formal specialisations from year2. Neither is established as more representative; take first-listed Bedrijfseconomie in the official2026 entrant structure, independently of UCR fit.

selection.assessment: Three independently tested directions are retained:business/economics/data;economics with institutions and public policy;economics and practical finance with quantitative methods. The original policy composition is reconstructed because a Walcheren-expedition history seminar has no specific economic-policy contribution and Comparative Constitutional Law lacked its formal gateway. Related theory and mathematics supply concrete foundations. Finance remains a methods-rich economics direction,not a complete specialist finance degree. All18 generator-eligible interests owned once;maximum three reached.

notes.text: Tilburg requires a combined economics-and-business curriculum, a 24-EC specialisation and a 12-EC thesis. The displayed external route is Bedrijfseconomie. The UCR options differ in business, data and public-policy emphasis and do not reproduce specialised management accounting, business administration, company law or sustainable finance. Optional independent research is additional to the displayed 180 EC.

audience.programmeDescription: Economie en Bedrijfseconomie at Tilburg University combines economic theory, accounting, finance, business and data analysis. Students choose an Economics or Business Economics specialisation after the common first year. This comparison shows the Dutch-language Bedrijfseconomie route.
audience.comparisonExplanation: The UCR options combine economics with business and data, public institutions and social policy, or practical finance and quantitative methods. Tilburg retains a more specialised accounting and business-economics sequence and a required 12-EC thesis. Shared rows show partial content relationships, not course equivalence.
